classification.difficultyReason: Identify the radius from its square and sketch origin-centred circles with exact intercepts, including surds.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly uses the origin-centred circle equation and the sketching method of Example 1; none requires translated-circle methods.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 derives x²+y²=r² using Pythagoras and assumes r>0. Example 1 identifies centre and radius, then sketches circles with exact axial intercept labels, including a surd radius. Page 3 reiterates the origin-centred equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the radius from its square and sketch origin-centred circles with exact intercepts, including surds.

classification.difficultyReason: Rearrange each equation into standard circle form, infer the radius, and use the axis intercepts to construct the sketch; these are routine linked algebraic and graphical procedures.

questions.mappingNote: Each assigned equation rearranges directly into the origin-centred form taught in Example 1; no translated-circle or completing-square method is required.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 derives x^2+y^2=r^2 and Example 1 sketches circles by identifying the origin as centre, taking the positive square root for the radius and labelling axis intercepts. Page 3 reinforces this circle form.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rearrange each equation into standard circle form, infer the radius, and use the axis intercepts to construct the sketch; these are routine linked algebraic and graphical procedures.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute each coordinate pair into the circle equation, including negative and surd coordinates.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly tests verification by substitution into x²+y²=100; the circle context supports the secondary skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 establishes that a point lies on an origin-centred circle precisely when its coordinates satisfy x²+y²=r². Page 3, Example 2, verifies individual points by substituting their coordinates and evaluating both squares.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute each coordinate pair into the circle equation, including negative and surd coordinates.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute each coordinate pair into a given circle equation, including negative coordinates and surds.

questions.mappingNote: Question 4 applies precisely this verification method to x²+y²=169. Substitution verification is the primary assessed skill; the circle equation supplies its context.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 establishes x²+y²=r². Page 3, Example 2, verifies points by substituting both coordinates into the circle equation, retaining parentheses around negative coordinates.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute each coordinate pair into a given circle equation, including negative coordinates and surds.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify translated-circle centres and radii, calculate exact intercepts and construct labelled sketches, including tangency.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts assess translated-circle sketches and intercepts directly matching Example 3; the general-circle skill is the closest and most advanced directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Read centre and radius from standard form. Following Example 3 on PDF page 4, substitute y=0 and x=0 separately, solve exactly for the intercepts, then sketch the circle and identify tangency where appropriate.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify translated-circle centres and radii, calculate exact intercepts and construct labelled sketches, including tangency.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of a supplied centre and radius into the standard circle equation.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly use the standard form with supplied centres and radii. Negative coordinates change the corresponding subtraction to addition; the zero coordinate in part d leaves $y^2$.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 gives the standard form $(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2$ for centre $(h,k)$ and radius $r$. Pages 4–5 reinforce reading the centre and squared radius from this form.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of a supplied centre and radius into the standard circle equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete two squares and interpret the resulting standard circle equation, including exact surd radii.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly practise Example 4's method. The standard form on PDF page 3 establishes the centre signs and radius squared; no graph is requested.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 on PDF page 5 groups the x- and y-terms, completes each square by adding the same constants on both sides, rewrites in standard form, then reads off the centre and positive radius.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete two squares and interpret the resulting standard circle equation, including exact surd radii.

classification.difficultyReason: Verify membership using the distance from the centre, then form the circle equation from the given centre and radius.

questions.mappingNote: Question 8 directly combines the distance criterion with substitution of the given centre and radius into the standard circle equation. The supplied reuse candidates have different givens and tasks, so none is source-equivalent.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 derives the translated-circle equation using the distance formula and states that a point lies on the circle when its distance from the centre equals the radius. Pages 2–3 demonstrate point verification; pages 4–5 reinforce identification of the centre and radius in standard form.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Verify membership using the distance from the centre, then form the circle equation from the given centre and radius.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the radius from the centre and a point on the circle, then substitute into standard form.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly assesses formation of a circle equation with a non-origin centre and an inferred radius. The supplied reuse candidates have different centres, points or parts and are not source-identical.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 derives the standard circle equation from the distance formula. Use the distance from the given centre to the origin as the radius, then substitute the centre and squared radius into standard form.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the radius from the centre and a point on the circle, then substitute into standard form.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer the radius from tangency to a coordinate axis, then substitute the centre and radius into the standard circle equation.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts require the translated-circle equation after determining the radius from tangency; circle-equation-general is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 gives the standard equation (x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2. Page 4 Example 3a connects touching an axis with the radius equalling the centre's perpendicular distance from that axis.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Infer the radius from tangency to a coordinate axis, then substitute the centre and radius into the standard circle equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Find a diameter and its midpoint, then use them to determine the radius, centre and circle equation.

questions.mappingNote: Part a uses the horizontal distance between the given endpoints; part b calculates their midpoint; part c uses that midpoint as the centre and half the diameter as the radius. The final assessed task matches circle-equation-general. Original midpoint teaching evidence remains required for compatibility review.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 gives the standard circle equation (x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2; page 4 applies centre and radius identification. The supplied teaching pages do not demonstrate calculating the midpoint of an interval.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find a diameter and its midpoint, then use them to determine the radius, centre and circle equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine distance and midpoint calculations to determine a circle from its diameter.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies the distance formula; part b averages endpoint coordinates; part c uses that midpoint as the centre and half the endpoint distance as the radius. The final directly assessed skill is forming a translated-circle equation.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 derives the distance relationship and standard circle equation. Pages 4–5 demonstrate identifying centre and radius and using standard form. Earlier teaching of the midpoint formula is absent from the supplied evidence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine distance and midpoint calculations to determine a circle from its diameter.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct substitution into a reciprocal rule, including negative and fractional inputs.

questions.mappingNote: All five parts assess numerical substitution and evaluation rather than graph construction, so substitute-into-expressions is the closest directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Substitute each nonzero x-value into y=1/x and simplify the reciprocal, retaining its sign. Page 7 supplies a value table for positive, negative and fractional inputs; page 10 retains the reciprocal form in the teaching examples.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution into a reciprocal rule, including negative and fractional inputs.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct substitution into a reciprocal rule, including division by negative numbers and fractions.

questions.mappingNote: All five parts assess evaluation of the supplied rule, rather than graph sketching or transformations, so substitution is the closest directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Substitute each nonzero x-value into y=a/x and simplify. Page 7 illustrates reciprocal values in native value tables; page 10 introduces y=a/x.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution into a reciprocal rule, including division by negative numbers and fractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute five signed integer or fractional values into a given reciprocal expression.

questions.mappingNote: Page 7 evaluates reciprocal values in tables; page 8 introduces y=-1/x as the reflected reciprocal graph. This question assesses numerical substitution rather than graph construction.
questions.methodNote: Substitute each given x-value into the reciprocal formula and evaluate exactly, retaining the sign.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute five signed integer or fractional values into a given reciprocal expression.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute five given values, including mixed numbers, into a reciprocal expression and evaluate exactly.

questions.mappingNote: Page 7 evaluates reciprocal functions through tables of values. Page 8 Example 6 uses this exact function and substitutes x=0 to calculate its y-intercept. Question 4 assesses the same substitution process with five other inputs.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the given x-value, evaluate the denominator, then evaluate the reciprocal. Retain exact fractions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute five given values, including mixed numbers, into a reciprocal expression and evaluate exactly.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch a scaled reciprocal curve, evaluate six ordinates and locate the corresponding points.

questions.mappingNote: Page 7 establishes reciprocal value tables and asymptotes. Page 10 explicitly teaches vertical stretching for y=a/x and demonstrates sketching a scaled reciprocal curve. Pages 8–9 provide related transformation and sketching context.
questions.methodNote: Use the basic reciprocal hyperbola and its coordinate-axis asymptotes, stretch ordinates by the numerator, substitute the given x-values, and plot the resulting coordinate pairs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch a scaled reciprocal curve, evaluate six ordinates and locate the corresponding points.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch a horizontally translated hyperbola, evaluate six inputs and plot the corresponding points.

questions.mappingNote: Page 7 establishes reciprocal values and asymptotes. Page 8 Example 6 models horizontal translation and substitution for the y-intercept. Page 10 Example 8 demonstrates translation two units left. These directly support both parts.
questions.methodNote: Translate the basic reciprocal graph horizontally, identify its asymptotes and intercepts, then substitute inputs and plot the resulting ordered pairs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch a horizontally translated hyperbola, evaluate six inputs and plot the corresponding points.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute five given values into a reciprocal expression and evaluate, including negative decimals and exact fractions.

questions.mappingNote: Page 10 generalises the reciprocal rule to y=a/x. Question 7 assesses evaluating this rule at supplied inputs; it does not require sketching or describing a transformation.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the given x-value into the reciprocal rule and evaluate exactly, as used to form the value tables on page 7 and find the y-intercept in Example 6 on page 8.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute five given values into a reciprocal expression and evaluate, including negative decimals and exact fractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute five given values into a rational expression, including decimals close to its undefined input.

questions.mappingNote: Page 7 constructs hyperbola value tables by substitution. Page 8 Example 6 substitutes x=0 into a denominator of x−3. Pages 9–10 establish translated and scaled hyperbolas; question 8 directly assesses numerical substitution rather than sketching.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the specified x-value, evaluate the denominator, then divide. Retain exact fractions where appropriate.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute five given values into a rational expression, including decimals close to its undefined input.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute five given values into a rational expression, evaluating small positive and negative decimal denominators.

questions.mappingNote: Question 9 directly assesses evaluation by substitution rather than sketching. Pages 8 and 10 establish horizontal translations, while page 7 supports the behaviour of values near the vertical asymptote.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the given x-value, evaluate the denominator first, then divide. Page 7 uses value tables to examine reciprocal values near zero; page 8 Example 6 explicitly substitutes x=0 into a translated reciprocal equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute five given values into a rational expression, evaluating small positive and negative decimal denominators.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch positive and negative reciprocal functions and calculate two points on each curve.

questions.mappingNote: Page 7 establishes reciprocal values and asymptotes; page 8 Example 5 supplies the explicitly referenced reflection method; page 10 explains stretching for y=a/x. Page 9's translation material was inspected but is not needed for these unshifted curves.
questions.methodNote: Use reciprocal-function shape and coordinate-axis asymptotes, substitute convenient nonzero inputs to obtain points, and apply reflection or stretching from the x-axis.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch positive and negative reciprocal functions and calculate two points on each curve.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch horizontally translated reciprocal graphs, including a reflection, and identify asymptotes and intercepts.

questions.mappingNote: Page 7 establishes reciprocal-graph features; page 8 Example 5 teaches reflection and Example 6 demonstrates horizontal translation, asymptotes and intercepts. Pages 9–10 reinforce transformations; Example 8 demonstrates a left translation. Question 11 directly assesses these methods.
questions.methodNote: Use the basic reciprocal graph, reflect in the x-axis where required, apply horizontal translation, identify asymptotes, and substitute x=0 for the y-intercept. A nonzero constant numerator gives no x-intercept.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch horizontally translated reciprocal graphs, including a reflection, and identify asymptotes and intercepts.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine vertical translation, reflection where required, asymptotes and exact intercept calculations to sketch four hyperbolas.

questions.mappingNote: Page 9 Example 7 directly models the vertical-translation, asymptote and intercept method for parts a, b and d. Page 8 Example 5 supplies the reflection used before the vertical translation in part c. Pages 7 and 10 establish basic branch behaviour and the general hyperbola family.
questions.methodNote: Use the basic rectangular hyperbola, reflection in the x-axis where needed, and vertical translation. Identify asymptotes, substitute y=0 to calculate the x-intercept, and note that x=0 is excluded.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine vertical translation, reflection where required, asymptotes and exact intercept calculations to sketch four hyperbolas.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch vertically translated reciprocal graphs, identifying asymptotes and calculating exact intercepts.

questions.mappingNote: Each part combines y=a/x with the vertical translation from Example 7: a has coefficient 2 and shift +1; b has coefficient 4 and shift -3; c has coefficient -12 and shift +4; d has coefficient 2 and shift -1. The negative coefficient in c reverses the branch orientation.
questions.methodNote: Page 7 establishes reciprocal branches and coordinate-axis asymptotes. Page 9 Example 7 translates a reciprocal graph vertically, identifies the new horizontal asymptote, substitutes y=0 to find the x-intercept and explains the absence of a y-intercept. Page 10 establishes y=a/x by vertical stretching.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch vertically translated reciprocal graphs, identifying asymptotes and calculating exact intercepts.

classification.difficultyReason: Equate a parabola and a line, solve the resulting quadratic and recover coordinate pairs.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess line–parabola intersections; the repeated root in c gives one point.
questions.methodNote: Example 9 equates the expressions for y, factorises the resulting quadratic and substitutes each x-value into the line.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Equate a parabola and a line, solve the resulting quadratic and recover coordinate pairs.

classification.difficultyReason: Reduce quadratic–linear pairs to factorisable quadratics, including non-monic cases and fractional coordinates.

questions.mappingNote: Each part assesses complete intersection coordinates rather than quadratic roots alone.
questions.methodNote: Use Example 9: eliminate y, factorise and substitute into the linear equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reduce quadratic–linear pairs to factorisable quadratics, including non-monic cases and fractional coordinates.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute horizontal, vertical and oblique line equations into circles, retaining exact surds.

questions.mappingNote: All parts assess line–circle intersections, with one point in a and two in b–d.
questions.methodNote: Example 10 substitutes the line into the circle and uses the line to pair coordinates correctly; page 3 establishes the circle equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute horizontal, vertical and oblique line equations into circles, retaining exact surds.

classification.difficultyReason: Eliminate the common quadratic terms from two circle equations, then substitute to obtain both exact intersection coordinates.

questions.mappingNote: The task assesses algebraic intersections of two circles. The supplied intersection skill is the closest catalogue match, supported by the general-circle skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 supplies the standard circle equation. Pages 13–15 find intersections by solving equations simultaneously, eliminating a variable and substituting to recover coordinates. Here subtraction eliminates the common squared terms, and substitution gives both signs of y.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Eliminate the common quadratic terms from two circle equations, then substitute to obtain both exact intersection coordinates.

classification.difficultyReason: Solve and sketch circle–line intersections, distinguishing two intersections, tangency and no real intersection.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–e have two points, f–h are tangencies and i–j have no intersection. The assessed skill includes both algebra and sketches.
questions.methodNote: Examples 10–12 substitute the line into the circle, factorise for intersections or use the discriminant for no real intersections, then illustrate graphically.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Solve and sketch circle–line intersections, distinguishing two intersections, tangency and no real intersection.

classification.difficultyReason: Rearrange the line and substitute into a translated circle, then solve a repeated-root quadratic to find the unique intersection.

questions.mappingNote: Rearranging the line as x=3y−7 avoids fractions while preserving the demonstrated substitution method. The resulting perfect square gives one point, as in Example 11.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 gives the translated-circle equation. Pages 13–15 solve intersections by substitution or elimination, reducing to a quadratic and substituting back into the line. Example 11 on page 14 demonstrates a repeated root giving one intersection.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rearrange the line and substitute into a translated circle, then solve a repeated-root quadratic to find the unique intersection.

classification.difficultyReason: Eliminate y, clear the nonzero denominator, factorise and sketch both hyperbola branches with the line.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts require algebraic intersection coordinates and a complete hyperbola–line sketch.
questions.methodNote: Example 13 equates the line and reciprocal expressions, multiplies by nonzero x, factorises and substitutes. Pages 7–8 establish reciprocal branches, asymptotes and reflection.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Eliminate y, clear the nonzero denominator, factorise and sketch both hyperbola branches with the line.

classification.difficultyReason: Solve two different intersection problems, select the points identified by the diagram and use their coordinates as perpendicular triangle dimensions.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly applies the demonstrated line–circle substitution and line–parabola elimination methods. The supplied diagram selects the first-quadrant points. Part b uses these coordinates as base and perpendicular height in the triangle area formula.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 establishes the origin-centred circle equation. Example 9 on page 13 equates expressions for y, factorises and substitutes to recover coordinates. Examples 10 and 11 on page 14 substitute the line into a circle equation. Page 15 continues the substitution/elimination method for graph intersections.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Solve two different intersection problems, select the points identified by the diagram and use their coordinates as perpendicular triangle dimensions.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute the line into a translated circle equation and use the resulting quadratic's negative discriminant to justify that there is no intersection.

questions.mappingNote: Question 8 directly applies Example 12's substitution and discriminant method to a circle centred at (5,0). No sketch is requested.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 gives the translated-circle equation. Pages 13–14 eliminate a variable by substitution to obtain a quadratic. Page 15, Example 12, proves that a line does not meet a circle by calculating a negative discriminant.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute the line into a translated circle equation and use the resulting quadratic's negative discriminant to justify that there is no intersection.

classification.difficultyReason: Form a quadratic containing a parameter, then solve discriminant conditions for one, two or no intersections.

questions.mappingNote: The question extends the supplied line–circle substitution and discriminant methods to an unknown line intercept. The most advanced directly assessed skill is finding parameter values using discriminant conditions; original teaching evidence for the parameter-inequality step remains required.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 establishes the circle equation. Page 13 connects the number of quadratic solutions with the number of intersections. Page 14 demonstrates substitution of a line into a circle equation for two intersections and tangency. Page 15 Example 12 uses a negative discriminant to establish no intersections. These pages do not demonstrate solving discriminant inequalities containing a parameter.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form a quadratic containing a parameter, then solve discriminant conditions for one, two or no intersections.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch eighteen linear half-planes, rearranging some inequalities and distinguishing included from excluded boundaries.

questions.mappingNote: Examples 14 and 15 on page 18 directly teach single linear half-planes; pages 17 and 19 explain boundary inclusion and horizontal or vertical boundaries. The assigned task assesses graphing linear inequality regions.
questions.methodNote: Sketch the boundary using intercepts or two points. Use a solid boundary for inclusive inequalities and a dashed boundary for strict inequalities. Rearrange with y as subject or test a point not on the boundary to choose the half-plane. Vertical inequalities are shaded left or right.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch eighteen linear half-planes, rearranging some inequalities and distinguishing included from excluded boundaries.

classification.difficultyReason: Derive a linear boundary from labelled intercepts or a y-intercept and another point, then combine the shaded side with solid or dashed boundary inclusion.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts reverse the half-plane construction taught on pages 17–18. Parts a and b supply the equation; c uses intercepts, and d uses the y-intercept and another point to establish the boundary.
questions.methodNote: Identify the boundary equation, use the shaded side to choose above or below, and include a solid boundary but exclude a dashed one. Page 18 Example 14 demonstrates y>=2x+1; Example 15 also demonstrates rearranging a linear boundary equation and checking a test point.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Derive a linear boundary from labelled intercepts or a y-intercept and another point, then combine the shaded side with solid or dashed boundary inclusion.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine taught half-plane sketches with routine simultaneous equations, select feasible boundary intersections and distinguish included from excluded corners; parts k and l require coordinating several boundaries.

questions.mappingNote: Pages 17–18 establish half-plane selection and boundary inclusion. Page 19 defines corner points and Example 16 handles horizontal and vertical boundaries, directly supporting g–i. Page 20 Example 17 models intersecting sloping boundaries, substitution and an excluded corner, directly supporting a–f and j–l. The source margin reference to Example 16, 17 is retained.
questions.methodNote: Sketch each boundary, use solid lines for included boundaries and dashed lines for strict inequalities, select each half-plane using its direction or a test point, and shade the common region. Solve boundary equations simultaneously for corner coordinates; mark excluded corners open.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine taught half-plane sketches with routine simultaneous equations, select feasible boundary intersections and distinguish included from excluded corners; parts k and l require coordinating several boundaries.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify several boundary equations and combine their shaded half-planes, distinguishing solid and dashed boundaries.

questions.mappingNote: Page 17 explains half-planes and dashed boundaries; page 18 demonstrates boundary equations and selecting sides; page 19 covers axis-parallel boundaries and intersections; page 20 demonstrates mixed strict and inclusive boundaries with an open corner. These methods apply individually to all six supplied regions.
questions.methodNote: Identify each boundary equation from intercepts or supplied points, select the shaded side, include solid boundaries and exclude dashed boundaries, then intersect the resulting half-planes.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify several boundary equations and combine their shaded half-planes, distinguishing solid and dashed boundaries.

classification.difficultyReason: Directly apply the taught circle form to identify centre and radius, then use the inequality sign to choose interior or exterior and boundary inclusion.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly apply Example 18 to circles with different centres, radii and inequality signs. The closest supplied taxonomy skill is circle-equation-general; interpreting the inequality is part of the source task.
questions.methodNote: Example 18 identifies the circle's centre and radius, interprets the inequality as a distance condition, and shades the interior or exterior. Solid boundaries are included; dashed boundaries are excluded.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Directly apply the taught circle form to identify centre and radius, then use the inequality sign to choose interior or exterior and boundary inclusion.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine the familiar reciprocal graph with the taught boundary-and-test-point method, applying the vertical comparison on both sides of the excluded vertical axis.

questions.mappingNote: Page 7 supplies the reciprocal graph, sample values and asymptotes. Pages 17–18 teach strict boundaries and shading above a graph; page 21 extends boundary-and-region reasoning to nonlinear curves. The catalogue has no reciprocal-inequality skill, so the closest region-sketching skill is combined with hyperbola transformations.
questions.methodNote: Sketch the boundary, use a dashed curve for a strict inequality, and select points above it by comparing y-coordinates or testing points. The reciprocal graph has two branches and excludes x=0.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine the familiar reciprocal graph with the taught boundary-and-test-point method, applying the vertical comparison on both sides of the excluded vertical axis.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the radius from each equation and sketch a circle centred at the origin; part b first requires division by 2.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess origin-centred circles. Part b requires simplifying the equation before applying the same method.
questions.methodNote: Use x²+y²=r², identify the positive radius, and sketch the origin-centred circle using its four axis intercepts. Page 2 Example 1 includes integer and surd radii; page 3 summarises the formula.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the radius from each equation and sketch a circle centred at the origin; part b first requires division by 2.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify translated circle centres and radii, calculate exact intercepts and sketch six circles.

questions.mappingNote: Page 3 supplies translated standard form; page 4 Example 3 demonstrates the intercept calculations and translated-circle sketches required by all six parts.
questions.methodNote: Read centre and radius from standard form. Find intercepts by setting y=0 and x=0, solve exactly and sketch the circle; recognise tangency and absence of intercepts.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify translated circle centres and radii, calculate exact intercepts and sketch six circles.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete two squares to identify each circle's centre and radius, including division by a common coefficient and fractional coefficients.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess conversion to standard circle form. Part c first requires division by 2 so both squared-variable coefficients are 1; the same completing-the-square method then applies with a fractional half-coefficient.
questions.methodNote: Page 5, Example 4: group the x-terms and y-terms, complete both squares by adding the same constants to both sides, write standard form, then read the centre and positive radius. Page 3 defines standard form.
